F U L C R U M ML Foundations 5 / 14Linear and logistic regression
Start here, and keep coming back here.
In applied work, a linear model with good features very often beats a neural network with bad ones.
Linear regression fits y = w·x + b  by minimising squared error. It has a closed-form solution.

Logistic regression passes that same linear score through a sigmoid to get a probability, and minimises cross-entropy.
Both are interpretable: each weight says how the prediction moves as one feature moves.
They are the correct baseline. A complex model that cannot beat logistic regression is telling you something.
F U L C R U M ML Foundations 6 / 14Gradient descent
Adam adapts a per-parameter step size and is a reasonable default. It is not magic; a badly scaled problem still trains badly.

query: How can we evaluate a machine learning model?
content:
three questions. Papers that seem impenetrable
usually become simple once you identify the
family, the loss and the optimiser.
A model family, the shape of function you will allow (a line, a tree, a
network).
A loss function, a number saying how wrong a given function is on your
data.
An optimiser, a procedure for reducing that number by adjusting
parameters.
Change any one and you get a different algorithm. That is genuinely most
of the field.
